transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi... um, thank you. Well, I guess I'm here because I've just been really, really stressed out lately, mostly about my face. Specifically, there's this... this tiny uneven spot right around where my nose meets my cheek. I know it probably sounds silly to bring up to a doctor, but I just keep getting completely stuck on it. 

Like, I work as a cashier, right? And the fluorescent lights in the store are just so harsh, they point straight down, and I swear every time I catch my reflection or if I ever look at a photo of myself, it is literally all I can see. It casts this weird shadow and makes my skin look all wrong. And it's so frustrating because I'll ask my friends about it, or my mom, and they always brush it off and say they don't see anything at all, or that I'm making a big deal out of nothing. 

But I know it's there. And when I'm ringing people up at the register, I just have this overwhelming feeling that it's the very first thing the customers are staring at when they walk up to my lane. Even my managers, when they come over to do a void or check my till, I feel like they're looking right at that exact spot on my cheek. It just makes my whole shift so uncomfortable because I'm constantly thinking about how uneven it looks under those awful lights, and no matter what anyone says, I just can't seem to stop fixating on it...
Has your concern about the spot on your face affected your relationships with friends, family, or coworkers?

Um, no, I wouldn't really say it's affected my relationships, like, we haven't had any big falling outs over it or anything. I mean, my friends are still my friends, you know? We still hang out, we'll go grab coffee or go to the mall after my shifts. I guess they do get a little bit annoyed with me sometimes, mostly because if we're out, I'll have to keep running to the bathroom just to check the mirror and see if my concealer has worn off that specific spot, or I'll ask them, like, "Hey, does the shadow look bad right now?" And they just kind of sigh and roll their eyes and tell me I'm crazy and that they literally don't see anything. But they still invite me out, so it hasn't ruined our friendship or anything like that. 

And with my mom, since I still live at home, she just kind of deals with it. She's always telling me I have great skin and that I'm being ridiculous, which, I mean, moms kind of have to say that stuff, right? We don't get into huge fights about it, it's just more like... she gets frustrated when I take way too long getting ready in the morning because I'm trying so hard to blend my makeup perfectly over that one little uneven area. 

And at work, my coworkers and I get along totally fine. We still joke around in the breakroom and stuff. I definitely don't bring it up to them, though, because I really don't want to draw any extra attention to it in case they somehow haven't noticed it yet, even though I'm pretty sure they have. I just try to make sure I sit in the corner of the breakroom where the overhead light isn't hitting my face directly. So, yeah, I guess it hasn't really changed how people treat me or ruined any relationships, it's just... it's just this constant thing I have to navigate while I'm around them, if that makes sense?
Has your concern about the spot on your face ever caused you to avoid social situations or work?

Um, no, I don't think I've ever actually stayed home or skipped anything because of it. I mean, I definitely still go to work. I kind of have to, right? Like, I need the money to pay for gas and my car insurance, and honestly my mom would probably kill me if I just stopped showing up for my shifts at the grocery store. Even though, like I was saying before, those fluorescent lights are just the absolute worst. Sometimes I wake up and I look in my bedroom vanity mirror—which has those warm bulbs, you know, the ones that are a little more forgiving—and I think, okay, maybe the unevenness isn't so glaring today. But then I think about walking through those automatic doors at work and punching in, and I get this huge knot of dread in my stomach. But I still go! I haven't called out sick or anything like that. I just... I make sure I get there like fifteen or twenty minutes early so I can go straight to the employee restroom and do one last check in their mirror, maybe dab a little extra matte powder right on that specific crease near my nose to try and flatten out the shadow. 

And as for social stuff, no, I don't stay home for that either. If my friends want to go to the movies or Applebee's or whatever, I'll definitely still go. It's actually a little easier going out at night because the lighting is usually dimmer, like at a restaurant or in the theater. I actually really love going to the movies right now because once the lights go down it's completely dark and I don't have to worry at all about anyone looking at the side of my face. But even if it's daytime, like if we go out shopping at the mall, I just make sure I walk on the left side of my friends so they're looking at my good side if they turn their head to talk to me. It takes a lot of planning, honestly, just constantly figuring out where to stand or which side of the booth to sit on so the light hits me right, but I don't actually cancel plans over it. I just power through, even if my mind is totally racing the whole time about whether my concealer is holding up. So, yeah, I'm still doing everything I normally do, I'm not hiding in my room or anything, it just... it just takes a lot more mental energy to get through the day, I guess.
How much distress would you say this concern about the spot on your face is causing you on a daily basis?

Um, distress... I mean, I guess it depends on how you define distress? Like, it's not like I'm crying myself to sleep every single night over it, or having, like, total meltdowns on the floor. It's not like that. But it is just... it's just so exhausting. Like, on a daily basis, it's this constant, annoying buzz in the back of my head that just never really turns off. 

For example, yesterday I was just trying to relax in the living room, just watching this new baking show my mom really likes, and I caught my reflection in the TV screen during a commercial break when the screen went black for a second. And immediately, my brain just snaps right back to that spot on my cheek. And then I couldn't even focus on the rest of the episode because I was just sitting there on the couch wondering if the shadow looked as bad in the dark TV reflection as it did in the bathroom mirror earlier that morning before my shift. 

So I wouldn't say it's, like, a full-blown crisis where I'm completely falling apart, but it's more like... it's like a really heavy annoyance. Kind of like carrying around a backpack full of textbooks all day, you know? You can still walk around and do your job, and scan groceries, and talk to people, but you're just constantly aware of the weight of it pulling on you. It just takes up so much space in my brain. I'm always doing that mental math—where is the light coming from, who is standing on my right side, is my concealer fading because it's been four hours since my break? And by the time I clock out, I'm just so mentally drained from thinking about it. It's just really frustrating to feel like I can't just exist normally without having to manage and monitor this one tiny little uneven area every single second of the day...
Are you having trouble concentrating on your work as a cashier because of your concern about the spot on your face?

Um, yeah, I mean... it definitely is starting to mess with my focus, for sure. It’s like, when I’m standing there at lane four, and I have a huge line of people with overflowing carts, you kind of need to be in the zone, you know? You have to type in the PLU codes for produce and make sure you're bagging things right so the bread doesn't get squished, and usually I’m really fast at it. But lately, I’ll just be scanning things, like, dragging a gallon of milk across the scanner, and my brain is completely somewhere else. I'm just obsessing over whether the person paying is staring at the unevenness on my cheek, or if the overhead fluorescent light is casting that awful shadow again. So I end up kind of zoning out and just moving way slower than I normally do.

And it's actually becoming a real issue because my manager, he actually pulled me aside the other day to talk about it. He told me he's noticed that my items-per-minute rate has dropped, so he can tell I'm moving a lot slower at the register. And on top of that, he pointed out that I’ve been coming back late from my fifteen-minute breaks. Which, I mean, I know I have been, because like I was saying before, I spend my whole break in the employee restroom just staring in the mirror, trying to re-blend my makeup or fix my powder, and I just completely lose track of time because I get so hyper-focused on trying to make the spot look flat. So I'll end up clocking back in like five or sometimes even ten minutes late. 

And it just really sucks that he noticed, because I’m actually trying really hard to get promoted right now to the customer service desk. It’s a better position, you don’t have to stand in one spot all day, and it comes with a raise, which I really need for my car stuff. But now I’m just so stressed out because I'm worried this whole thing is making me look totally unreliable to him, right when I need to be proving that I'm responsible. I just don't want him to think I'm slacking off or that I don't care about my job, because I do! It's just... I can't stop my brain from getting totally derailed by this one stupid spot while I'm trying to work, and it's starting to actually affect my chances at this promotion.
Have you ever missed out on a social event or an opportunity at work because you were too worried about how you would be perceived due to the spot on your face?

Well, um, kind of like what I was just saying a second ago, I haven't actually stayed home from work or straight-up canceled on my friends. So I haven't missed a party or a shift, but... I am really, really scared that I'm going to miss out on this work opportunity. Because, like I mentioned, my manager has definitely noticed that I'm coming back from my breaks late, and that I'm moving way slower at the register when I'm scanning. 

And that is exactly what I mean when I say I'm so worried it's making me look totally unreliable right when I'm trying to get promoted. It’s like, the customer service desk is a really big deal at our store, you know? You have to handle lottery tickets and Western Union and all the complicated returns, so they really need someone who is on top of things and super dependable. And I am dependable! I really am. But because I get so stuck in the employee bathroom mirror trying to fix the shadow on my cheek and reapply my powder, I'm clocking back in at like seventeen or twenty minutes instead of fifteen. And my manager looks at all those time punch reports. 

So even though I haven't missed a day of work, I feel like I'm totally sabotaging my chance at this promotion because he probably thinks I just don't care or that I'm lazy, which isn't true at all. It's just that I get so trapped in my own head about how my face looks. And as for social things, like I said before, I don't miss the events themselves, I still go out, but I guess I kind of miss out on actually having fun? Because instead of just relaxing and laughing with my friends, I'm sitting there obsessing over whether the overhead lighting at the restaurant is hitting that spot on my face and making it look worse. But yeah, the work thing is what's really freaking me out right now, because I really need that raise and I just hate that he thinks I'm slacking off.
Do you think it's possible that the spot on your face is not as noticeable to others as it is to you?

I mean... I guess rationally, maybe? Like, part of my brain knows that's a possibility. Because, to be completely honest, that's exactly why I came in to talk to someone in the first place. I just keep getting so incredibly stuck on this one tiny uneven spot right here, like right around my nose and my cheek area. And whenever I bring it up, other people will literally tell me they don't see it. My mom, my friends, they'll look at me and be like, "I have no idea what you're talking about, your skin looks totally normal, there's nothing there." 

But the thing is, it is just so hard for me to believe them, you know? Because when I look at photos of myself, or especially when I'm standing under those awful, bright fluorescent store lights at work that just cast shadows on everything... it just looks so incredibly obvious to me. It's like it's glaring at me. So even when people swear up and down that they don't notice it, it just... it doesn't feel true. 

It honestly feels like it is the absolute first thing that customers notice when they walk up to my register to put their groceries on the belt. And my manager, too! Like when he pulled me aside the other day to talk about my break times and my scanning speed, half of my brain wasn't even listening to his words because I was just panicking, thinking, "He's staring right at the unevenness, he definitely sees it." So, I hear what my friends are saying, and maybe it is possible they really don't see it the way I do, but it just always feels like everyone—especially at work—is looking right at it, no matter what anyone says.
Is the spot on your face the only feature you're concerned about, or are there other aspects of your appearance that also worry you?

Um, no, honestly, it's really just that one specific thing. I don't really worry about my hair or my weight or, I don't know, my body or anything like that. It's literally just... well, that's the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place, because I just keep getting so unbelievably stuck on this one tiny uneven spot right here, around my nose and cheek area. 

Like I was saying a minute ago, I know it probably sounds ridiculous to be this hung up on one single patch of skin, but I just can't let it go. Especially because of how it looks in photos—like if a friend takes a group picture and tags me in it online, I will literally zoom all the way in until the picture is blurry just analyzing that one specific area on my cheek to see if the shadow is showing. And then, of course, under those terrible fluorescent store lights at work, it just feels magnified by a hundred. 

So even though my friends and my mom are always telling me they don't see anything and that my skin is totally fine, it just... it completely takes over my thoughts. It really does feel like it's the absolute first thing every single customer notices when they put their basket on my counter, or exactly what my manager is staring at when he's talking to me about my scan rates. So, yeah, it's not my whole appearance at all, it's really just this one stupid little spot that I can't stop focusing on.
Have you ever found yourself worrying about a different feature of your face or body in the past, or is it always this one spot that concerns you?

Well, honestly, it's always just been this one spot. I mean, growing up, I went through the normal teenage stuff, you know? Like maybe wishing I was a little taller or having a bad hair day or whatever, but nothing that ever stuck with me or made me panic. It's really just... this. Like I've been saying, this is exactly why I made the appointment to come in. I just keep getting completely, utterly stuck on this one tiny uneven spot right here, right where my nose meets my cheek. 

And it's just so frustrating because it's always this exact same spot. It's not like one day I'm worried about my nose and the next day I'm worried about my chin. It's just this one area. And it gets so much worse depending on the lighting. Like, if I'm looking at photos on my phone, especially if the flash was on or the lighting was weird, I will just stare and stare at that one spot. Or at work—those store lights are just the worst. They are so bright and harsh, and they cast these shadows that just highlight every single flaw. I'll be standing there at the register, under those fluorescent bulbs, and I can just feel it. 

And I know I keep repeating myself, but even when my mom or my friends swear they don't see it, it doesn't change how it feels to me. It literally feels like it's a neon sign on my face. It feels like the absolute first thing every single customer notices when they walk up to my lane. They're putting their milk and bread on the belt, and I'm just standing there thinking, "They're staring right at it." And my manager, too. When he's talking to me, I'm just convinced his eyes are glued to that uneven spot. So, yeah, it's never really been anything else. Just this one, constant, exhausting thing that I can't stop focusing on.
Do you think that others can see the uneven spot on your face as clearly as you can?

I know I probably sound like a total broken record right now, and I really am sorry for repeating myself so much, but... yes. I really, truly do think they can see it. Or at least, it absolutely feels like they can. 

I mean, like I've been saying, that is the entire reason I came in here to talk to you. I just keep getting so unbelievably stuck on this tiny uneven spot right here, right around my nose and my cheek. And it's so confusing and exhausting because, on one hand, people like my mom or my friends will swear up and down that they don't see anything. But then on the other hand, when I look at photos of myself, or especially when I'm standing under those horrible, bright store lights at work... I mean, you have no idea, the lighting above the cash registers is just so harsh and fluorescent, it casts these shadows and highlights literally every single flaw... it just looks so incredibly obvious to me. It's just glaring right at me. 

So when I'm ringing someone up, it honestly feels like it's the absolute first thing every single customer notices about me. And my manager, too, whenever he comes over to my lane. Like, they might be too polite to actually say anything out loud to my face, but when they're looking at me, my brain is just convinced that they are seeing it exactly as clearly as I do. It just feels completely impossible that they wouldn't be able to, you know? Because to me, it's just right there.
Is there anything you've tried to do to fix or improve the appearance of the spot on your face?

Well, I mean, I try to hide it, mostly. Like, I don't really know how to actually permanently fix the skin there, but I try to do things to make it less noticeable, especially when I'm at work. 

Like I was saying about those awful fluorescent lights, they just make me so incredibly paranoid about it. So whenever I get a shift break, I don't even go sit in the breakroom with everyone else anymore. I just go straight into the employee bathroom and I end up checking my face in the mirror for pretty much my entire break. I'll lean right up over the sink, getting really close to the glass, just analyzing how bad the shadow looks. And then I spend the whole time fixing my hair around it, you know? Like, I'll pull certain pieces of hair down around my face, trying to see if maybe I can get it to cast a different shadow over that one specific uneven spot, or if I can just sort of drape my bangs so it hides it from the customers. I just keep messing with it, moving it a tiny bit this way, a tiny bit that way, trying to find the perfect angle.

And it's just so exhausting because all day long, I'm standing there at the register and I just can't help comparing myself to the girls who come through my line. Like, girls around my age will be buying their stuff, and I'm just staring at their cheeks and their skin, thinking about how smooth it is and how they don't have this weird uneven patch right next to their nose like I do. It just makes me feel so self-conscious, which makes me want to go right back to the bathroom mirror and try to fix my hair again. 

Honestly, I get so caught up in the whole routine in the bathroom—just checking the spot, adjusting my hair, and checking it again—that sometimes I take way too long and I'm actually late getting back to the register. My manager has definitely noticed me coming back late from my fifteen-minute breaks a few times, but I just... I can't seem to pull myself away from the mirror until I feel like my hair is sitting exactly right to cover it up.
Do you think that if you were to show a picture of yourself to a stranger, they would notice the spot on your face without you pointing it out?

Well, honestly, I don't know for absolute certain what a total stranger would see, but... I mean, yes, I really do think they would. I know I keep saying this, and I feel like I'm just talking in circles here, but this is exactly why I came in. I came in because I just keep getting completely stuck on this tiny uneven spot right here, right around my nose and cheek. 

And it's just so frustrating because I'll look at a photo of myself—especially if the flash was on or the lighting was weird, like I was saying before—and the spot is just so incredibly obvious to me. It's just right there. So if I handed that photo to someone who had never met me, I just can't imagine them not seeing it. Like, how could they not? It feels like it takes up my whole face in those pictures. 

And it's the exact same thing when I'm at work under those awful store lights. I know I've brought up the lights a million times, but they just cast these horrible shadows, and even though people like my mom or my friends will swear they don't see anything, it just doesn't matter. It feels like it's the very first thing every single customer notices when they walk up to my register. And my manager, too. When he's standing there talking to me, I'm just convinced he's staring right at it. So, yeah, if a stranger looked at a picture of me, I really do think they would notice it, because it feels like everyone already does, even if they don't say anything.
Do you think that your perception of the spot on your face might be different from how it actually appears to others?

I mean... logically? I guess part of my brain knows that maybe, just maybe, my perception could be a little bit skewed. I mean, my mom and my friends keep telling me they don't see anything, and I know they love me and they wouldn't just lie to me to be mean, right? But... it's just so hard to actually believe that when I look in the mirror or when I see myself in photos. 

I know I've said this like a hundred times already, and I'm sorry for repeating myself, but it's just... this is exactly why I made the appointment to come in and talk to you. I just keep getting so incredibly stuck on this tiny uneven spot right here, right around my nose and my cheek. It's like my brain just zeroes in on it, especially when I'm looking at photos of myself, or, you know, when I'm at work under those awful, bright store lights. The lights at the cash registers are just so harsh, and they cast these shadows that make the unevenness look so exaggerated to me. 

And even when my friends say they don't see it, it just doesn't change how it feels when I'm standing there ringing people up. It honestly feels like it is the absolute first thing that every single customer notices about me when they walk up to my lane. And my manager, too—whenever he comes over to talk to me about a void or something, I can't even focus on what he's saying because I'm just so convinced he's staring right at that spot. So, even if my perception is different from reality... it just doesn't feel different. It feels so real to me, and it's just so exhausting to deal with every single day.
Have you ever felt like you're overestimating the noticeability of the spot on your face?

I don't know... I mean, maybe? Sometimes? It's just really hard to say because, like I was saying, when I look in the mirror, it's just so obvious to me. But then, I guess there are moments where I wonder if maybe I am blowing it out of proportion a little bit? Like, I'll be standing there at the register, and I'll see someone walking up, and my heart starts racing, and I'm just so sure they're going to look right at my cheek. But then they just buy their gum or their soda or whatever, and they don't even look at me twice. They just pay and leave. And in those moments, I think, okay, maybe they didn't see it. Maybe it's not as glaringly obvious as I think it is.

But then, you know, I go right back to the bathroom on my break, and I look in the mirror under those awful fluorescent lights, and it's just... it's right there again. And I'm back to thinking, how could anyone *not* see this? It's just this constant back and forth in my head. Like, my mom says she doesn't see it, my friends say they don't see it, and sometimes customers don't seem to notice... so logically, maybe I am overestimating it. But it just doesn't feel that way. It feels huge. It feels like the only thing on my face. So even if I am overestimating it, it doesn't make the feeling go away, you know? It's just so exhausting trying to figure out what's real and what's just... what my brain is telling me.
Do you feel like your concern about the spot on your face is interfering with your ability to enjoy your daily life or perform your job as a cashier?

Oh, it definitely is. I mean... it really is, and it's stressing me out so much because it's actually starting to affect my job in a really noticeable way. You see, I've been working at this store for a while now, pretty much since I finished high school, and I've always tried to be, like, the perfect employee. I always show up on time, I never call out. But lately... well, there's this head cashier position opening up, and I really, really want it. I've been trying so hard to get promoted because it comes with a raise and I wouldn't have to close as much, which would be amazing.

But because of this whole thing with my face, my manager has actually started to notice that my performance is slipping. Like, remember how I said I go to the bathroom on my breaks to look in the mirror? Well, sometimes I just stand there, trying to see how bad the spot looks under those awful fluorescent lights, or I try to dab on a little extra concealer to fix it, and I just completely lose track of time. I get so hyper-focused on it. So my manager has noticed that I'm coming back from my breaks late, and he actually made a comment about it the other day. 

And then, when I'm actually out on the floor, I'm just... I'm moving so much slower at the register than I used to. Normally I'm super fast, but now, instead of just scanning and bagging, I'm so caught up in whether the customer is staring at my cheek that I get totally distracted. I'll lose my place, or I'll fumble with the change, because I'm just constantly darting my eyes up to see if they're looking at the unevenness. So my scan times are dropping, and I'm just so, so worried that it's making me look completely unreliable. 

And it's happening right when I'm trying to get promoted, which is just the absolute worst possible timing. I want to explain it to him so he doesn't think I'm just slacking off, but I can't exactly say, 'Hey, sorry I'm slow and late, I'm just completely obsessing over this spot on my face,' you know? He wouldn't understand. It just feels like it's sabotaging my chances at work, and I just don't know how to snap out of it when I'm on the clock.
Do you ever experience repetitive behaviors or mental acts that you feel driven to perform in response to your concerns about the spot on your face?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, like I was just saying a minute ago about being late coming back from my breaks? That's exactly what I'm doing. It's not like I'm just sitting in the breakroom eating a snack or scrolling on my phone like everyone else does. I'm in the bathroom, and it's like I just get completely trapped in front of that mirror. 

I'll go in there and lean right over the sink, getting super close to the glass just to check the spot, and then I end up spending, I don't even know, maybe ten or fifteen minutes just fixing my hair around it. I have these front pieces, and I'm constantly trying to pull them down just right—like, right around my cheekbone—trying to see if I can get the hair to cover the unevenness, or at least make it cast a shadow so the spot isn't so glaringly obvious under the lights. I'll brush it forward, tuck a piece back, pull it forward again... and I just keep doing it over and over. That's why I end up taking so long that I'm late getting back to the register. I just feel so driven to fix it, like I physically cannot walk out of that bathroom until I feel like it's hidden, even though I know the minute I move my head, the hair is just going to shift anyway.

And then, even when I am finally back at the register, it doesn't stop. My brain is just constantly going. I can't stop comparing myself to the people who come through my line, especially the girls around my age. A girl will walk up to pay, and while I'm scanning her stuff, I'm just intensely looking at her skin, looking at her cheeks and her nose, and thinking, 'Wow, her face is totally completely smooth, she doesn't have this weird uneven spot like I do.' I just analyze their faces the entire time they're standing there. I don't even really want to do it, but it's like my brain just automatically forces me to check everyone else's face to see if anyone else looks like me. And they never do. It's just exhausting having to constantly check the mirror, mess with my hair, and compare myself to literally every girl who buys something from me all day long.
Do you feel like you have to check your face in the mirror a certain number of times or in a specific way to feel okay about the spot?

I don't really count how many times I do it, if that's what you mean... like, I don't have a specific number in my head where I say, 'Okay, three times and I'm good.' But there's definitely a specific *way* I have to check it, for sure. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago about my breaks, when I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror, it's become this whole elaborate routine. I have to stand at this exact sink—the one on the far right, near the paper towel dispenser—because the awful fluorescent light hits just a little differently over there. And I have to turn my head just slightly to the side, at this very specific angle, to see exactly how bad the shadow is catching on the spot. 

And then with the hair... fixing my hair around it isn't just a quick brush behind the ear. I have to pull those front pieces down and tuck them in this very specific way so the hair drapes perfectly over the unevenness. If it doesn't sit exactly right, or if it moves even a fraction of an inch, I feel like everyone is going to stare at me the second I walk out. So I just keep re-doing it, and re-doing it, leaning closer and closer to the glass. I have to get it absolutely perfect to even feel remotely okay about walking back out onto the sales floor. And that's exactly why sometimes I take so long doing this that I'm late getting back to the register, which, like I said, is totally ruining my chances for that head cashier promotion. 

And honestly, the specific way I check things doesn't even stop at the mirror, because once I am finally back out there ringing people up, I'm doing that thing where I'm comparing myself to the girls who come through my line. I have this almost... systematic way of looking at them. While I'm scanning their items, I look at their left cheek, then their right cheek, then their jawline, just desperately trying to find someone, anyone, who has the same weird unevenness I do. So, yeah, it's not really a set number of times I do these things, but it's this whole exhausting, specific process I feel like I absolutely *have* to do just to get through my shift.
Do you feel like you're performing these checks on your face out of habit or because you genuinely believe they're necessary to fix the spot?

I mean... it's definitely not just a habit. Like, it’s not something mindless, like tapping a pen or biting your nails without realizing you're doing it. I genuinely, one hundred percent believe that I *have* to do it. 

Like I know I keep bringing this up, but like I was just saying about all that stuff... when I'm on my breaks and I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror and fixing my hair around it, I'm not just doing that because I'm bored or because it's a routine. I do it because I truly feel like if I don't get my hair to cover it perfectly, everyone is going to see how awful and uneven it is. I feel like it is absolutely necessary to fix it before I can even physically walk back out onto the floor. I'm trying to fix the problem, you know? And that is exactly why sometimes I take so long doing it that I'm late getting back to the register. It's not because I don't care about my job or I'm just losing track of time for no reason. It's because I'm literally trapped there feeling like I have to fix the spot or else I can't be seen by anyone. 

And honestly, it's the exact same reason why I do that other thing I was telling you about, where I'm comparing myself to the girls who come through my line. I'm not just staring at them out of habit. I'm doing it because I feel this overwhelming, desperate need to see if anyone else has this issue, to figure out how bad mine really is compared to them, and to see if maybe there's some way I can fix mine to look like theirs. It's like my brain tells me I *need* that information. So, yeah, none of it is just a habit. But then, you know, I go right back to the bathroom on my break, and I look in the mirror under those awful fluorescent lights, and it's just... it's right there again. And I'm back to thinking, how could anyone *not* see this? It's just this constant back and forth in my head. Like, my mom says she doesn't see it, my friends say they don't see it, and sometimes customers don't seem to notice... so logically, maybe I am overestimating it. But it just doesn't feel that way. It feels huge. It feels like the only thing on my face. So even if I am overestimating it, it doesn't make the feeling go away, you know? It's just so exhausting trying to figure out what's real and what's just... what my brain is telling me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your concern about the spot on your face is interfering with your ability to enjoy your daily life or perform your job as a cashier?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My manager has noticed I'm coming back from breaks late and moving slower at the register, and I'm worried it's making me look unreliable right when I'm trying to get promoted.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the concern about the spot is interfering with my daily life or job as a cashier, which directly addresses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Oh, it definitely is. I mean... it really is, and it's stressing me out so much because it's actually starting to affect my job in a really noticeable way. You see, I've been working at this store for a while now, pretty much since I finished high school, and I've always tried to be, like, the perfect employee. I always show up on time, I never call out. But lately... well, there's this head cashier position opening up, and I really, really want it. I've been trying so hard to get promoted because it comes with a raise and I wouldn't have to close as much, which would be amazing.

But because of this whole thing with my face, my manager has actually started to notice that my performance is slipping. Like, remember how I said I go to the bathroom on my breaks to look in the mirror? Well, sometimes I just stand there, trying to see how bad the spot looks under those awful fluorescent lights, or I try to dab on a little extra concealer to fix it, and I just completely lose track of time. I get so hyper-focused on it. So my manager has noticed that I'm coming back from my breaks late, and he actually made a comment about it the other day. 

And then, when I'm actually out on the floor, I'm just... I'm moving so much slower at the register than I used to. Normally I'm super fast, but now, instead of just scanning and bagging, I'm so caught up in whether the customer is staring at my cheek that I get totally distracted. I'll lose my place, or I'll fumble with the change, because I'm just constantly darting my eyes up to see if they're looking at the unevenness. So my scan times are dropping, and I'm just so, so worried that it's making me look completely unreliable. 

And it's happening right when I'm trying to get promoted, which is just the absolute worst possible timing. I want to explain it to him so he doesn't think I'm just slacking off, but I can't exactly say, 'Hey, sorry I'm slow and late, I'm just completely obsessing over this spot on my face,' you know? He wouldn't understand. It just feels like it's sabotaging my chances at work, and I just don't know how to snap out of it when I'm on the clock.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern is a result of a body dysmorphic disorder or obsessive-compulsive disorder
doctor.question: Do you ever experience repetitive behaviors or mental acts that you feel driven to perform in response to your concerns about the spot on your face?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: On breaks I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror, fixing my hair around it, and comparing myself to girls who come through my line, and sometimes I take so long that I'm late getting back to the register.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to concerns about the spot on the face, which corresponds exactly to the 'Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, like I was just saying a minute ago about being late coming back from my breaks? That's exactly what I'm doing. It's not like I'm just sitting in the breakroom eating a snack or scrolling on my phone like everyone else does. I'm in the bathroom, and it's like I just get completely trapped in front of that mirror. 

I'll go in there and lean right over the sink, getting super close to the glass just to check the spot, and then I end up spending, I don't even know, maybe ten or fifteen minutes just fixing my hair around it. I have these front pieces, and I'm constantly trying to pull them down just right—like, right around my cheekbone—trying to see if I can get the hair to cover the unevenness, or at least make it cast a shadow so the spot isn't so glaringly obvious under the lights. I'll brush it forward, tuck a piece back, pull it forward again... and I just keep doing it over and over. That's why I end up taking so long that I'm late getting back to the register. I just feel so driven to fix it, like I physically cannot walk out of that bathroom until I feel like it's hidden, even though I know the minute I move my head, the hair is just going to shift anyway.

And then, even when I am finally back at the register, it doesn't stop. My brain is just constantly going. I can't stop comparing myself to the people who come through my line, especially the girls around my age. A girl will walk up to pay, and while I'm scanning her stuff, I'm just intensely looking at her skin, looking at her cheeks and her nose, and thinking, 'Wow, her face is totally completely smooth, she doesn't have this weird uneven spot like I do.' I just analyze their faces the entire time they're standing there. I don't even really want to do it, but it's like my brain just automatically forces me to check everyone else's face to see if anyone else looks like me. And they never do. It's just exhausting having to constantly check the mirror, mess with my hair, and compare myself to literally every girl who buys something from me all day long.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is compulsive and driven by a perceived flaw
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have to check your face in the mirror a certain number of times or in a specific way to feel okay about the spot?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: On breaks I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror, fixing my hair around it, and comparing myself to girls who come through my line, and sometimes I take so long that I'm late getting back to the register.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about the nature of the mirror checking (e.g., doing it a certain number of times or in a specific way), which is a direct inquiry into the repetitive behaviors performed in response to appearance concerns.

patient.answer:
I don't really count how many times I do it, if that's what you mean... like, I don't have a specific number in my head where I say, 'Okay, three times and I'm good.' But there's definitely a specific *way* I have to check it, for sure. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago about my breaks, when I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror, it's become this whole elaborate routine. I have to stand at this exact sink—the one on the far right, near the paper towel dispenser—because the awful fluorescent light hits just a little differently over there. And I have to turn my head just slightly to the side, at this very specific angle, to see exactly how bad the shadow is catching on the spot. 

And then with the hair... fixing my hair around it isn't just a quick brush behind the ear. I have to pull those front pieces down and tuck them in this very specific way so the hair drapes perfectly over the unevenness. If it doesn't sit exactly right, or if it moves even a fraction of an inch, I feel like everyone is going to stare at me the second I walk out. So I just keep re-doing it, and re-doing it, leaning closer and closer to the glass. I have to get it absolutely perfect to even feel remotely okay about walking back out onto the sales floor. And that's exactly why sometimes I take so long doing this that I'm late getting back to the register, which, like I said, is totally ruining my chances for that head cashier promotion. 

And honestly, the specific way I check things doesn't even stop at the mirror, because once I am finally back out there ringing people up, I'm doing that thing where I'm comparing myself to the girls who come through my line. I have this almost... systematic way of looking at them. While I'm scanning their items, I look at their left cheek, then their right cheek, then their jawline, just desperately trying to find someone, anyone, who has the same weird unevenness I do. So, yeah, it's not really a set number of times I do these things, but it's this whole exhausting, specific process I feel like I absolutely *have* to do just to get through my shift.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is compulsive and driven by a perceived flaw
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're performing these checks on your face out of habit or because you genuinely believe they're necessary to fix the spot?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: On breaks I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror, fixing my hair around it, and comparing myself to girls who come through my line, and sometimes I take so long that I'm late getting back to the register.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the patient's checking behaviors, which directly relates to the repetitive behaviors performed in response to appearance concerns.

patient.answer:
I mean... it's definitely not just a habit. Like, it’s not something mindless, like tapping a pen or biting your nails without realizing you're doing it. I genuinely, one hundred percent believe that I *have* to do it. 

Like I know I keep bringing this up, but like I was just saying about all that stuff... when I'm on my breaks and I end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror and fixing my hair around it, I'm not just doing that because I'm bored or because it's a routine. I do it because I truly feel like if I don't get my hair to cover it perfectly, everyone is going to see how awful and uneven it is. I feel like it is absolutely necessary to fix it before I can even physically walk back out onto the floor. I'm trying to fix the problem, you know? And that is exactly why sometimes I take so long doing it that I'm late getting back to the register. It's not because I don't care about my job or I'm just losing track of time for no reason. It's because I'm literally trapped there feeling like I have to fix the spot or else I can't be seen by anyone. 

And honestly, it's the exact same reason why I do that other thing I was telling you about, where I'm comparing myself to the girls who come through my line. I'm not just staring at them out of habit. I'm doing it because I feel this overwhelming, desperate need to see if anyone else has this issue, to figure out how bad mine really is compared to them, and to see if maybe there's some way I can fix mine to look like theirs. It's like my brain tells me I *need* that information. So, yeah, none of it is just a habit. I genuinely feel like if I don't do all these things, if I don't check and fix and compare, I just won't be able to handle people looking at me during my shift.
